title: What it’s like to work at an AI-native company
author: Elena Verna
summary: Elena Verna, a growth executive at Lovable, offers field notes on what changes when an organization is built on the assumption that AI is part of everything, while stressing that she has only one data point. Her central claim is that the difference is not tactical productivity but a changed organization: flat titles, senior people content as individual contributors, and deep suspicion of meetings. She argues that much of what was historically called management may have been the labor of moving information and decisions through a hierarchy that is no longer needed. The piece balances this with what is hard, including an exhausting pace, blurred ownership, and a constant state of reorganization, and with what is strange, such as employees eager to automate their own jobs and AI agents managed by human agent parents. Verna concludes that as AI strips away the mechanics of work, the company depends more on human judgment, and she warns that these practices work as a system rather than as transplantable tips.
points: Titles carry status, access, information, and permission, so removing them exposes how much organizational politics they encode.
Verna suggests management will be rethought most, shifting from routing information and approvals to creating context, raising the quality bar, and developing people.
When velocity is high and correction is fast, the cost of being wrong can fall below the cost of meetings chasing a perfect decision.
High agency has a shadow side: it can become a flattering name for duplicated work and unclear accountability.
Lovable assigns each internal AI agent a human agent parent responsible for its output quality, turning repetitive expertise into maintained tools.
quotes: What’s been really strange is seeing the org itself change based on the assumption that AI is part of everything: what jobs look like, how people work together, who makes decisions, how information flows, and even what it means to be good at your job.

What I didn’t fully appreciate before is how much organizational machinery and politics are attached to titles. They’re not just labels for your job. They’re status, access, information, and even permission.

Not that managers will disappear, but a surprising amount of what we historically called ‘management’ may have actually been the work required to make information and decisions travel through a hierarchy that is no longer needed.
Actually, the cost of being wrong is usually lower than the cost of endless meetings trying to make the perfect decision (which doesn’t even exist).

There are definitely moments where ‘high agency’ is just a flattering way of describing duplicated work, unclear accountability, or someone stomping on somebody else’s toes. Sometimes the chaos produces a better outcome. Sometimes it’s just chaos.
So a reorg is less likely to be interpreted as ‘something went wrong’ and more as ‘we learned something new.
The weird paradox is that the more AI removes the mechanics of work, the more the company seems to depend on human judgment.
